subject: [RFC PATCH 00/18] mm: read the page cache without folio references

reviews.author: Kiryl Shutsemau (author)
reviews.summary:
The author acknowledges that contention between CPUs is a significant issue, but argues that an atomic operation on a cache line already owned by the CPU is cheap, and that the hot marking mechanism in the patch series looks for reads of the same folio, which are what cause the contention. No fix is planned.

Author acknowledges that marking more folios as PG_rcu_free is not free and may require a better heuristic, but plans to gather data from real workloads before revising the patch.
reviews.raw_body:
They do, but an atomic on a cache line the CPU already owns is cheap.
The cost is the line bouncing between CPUs, and that takes many reads of
the same folio, which is what the hot marking looks for.

Single thread, 16-byte pread() of one page, mitigations=off: base does
7.4-7.7M reads/s, the series 7.7-8.0M.  Dropping the reference saves a
few percent when nothing contends.  With 64 threads on the same page,
base falls to 17M reads/s in total and the series does 220M.

---

Marking more is not free either.

A flagged folio goes back to the page allocator only after a grace
period, so what reclaim and compaction free is not usable right away,
and they have to work harder to keep up.

I am all for finding a better heuristic. But it is hard balance.

I will get back with data from real workloads.

-- 
  Kiryl Shutsemau / Kirill A. Shutemov

reviews.author: Linus Torvalds
reviews.summary: Reviewer questioned the relevance of the benchmark results, stating that the 'often stays the same' claim only holds for a specific and contrived test case, and likely does not reflect real-world usage.
reviews.raw_body:
This seems silly. That "often stays the same" is only true for the
pointless benchmark, no?

I don't think it's ever true in any real load.

            Linus

2026-10-20.patch_summary: This patch series introduces a new mechanism to read from the page cache without taking a reference on folios, which can lead to refcount bouncing between CPUs. The approach involves marking accessed folios as PG_rcu_free and deferring their free until an RCU grace period. This allows for more efficient handling of small reads and reduces the overhead of lock contention. The series includes 18 patches that implement this new mechanism in various parts of the Linux kernel, including filemap_read(), shmem, and memory_failure(). The goal is to improve performance on systems with many CPUs by reducing the number of references taken on folios and minimizing the impact of refcount bouncing.

reviews.author: Kiryl Shutsemau (author)
reviews.summary: Author acknowledges that the prev_pos store in a shared struct file is problematic and will replace the patch with an alternative solution.
reviews.raw_body:
Right. The patch is bogus, not only the commit message.

It is worse than useless: for random reads prev_pos changes every time,
so the compare reads the shared line and then writes it anyway.
Bisecting a RocksDB slowdown led here: with patches 1-12 it runs at base
speed, this one costs 4-5% at 16-64 threads.

The store itself does matter in a real load.  RocksDB threads pread()
through one fd per SST file, opened with POSIX_FADV_RANDOM.  With the
folio refcount gone, the prev_pos store on that shared struct file is
what they fight over next.

For an FMODE_RANDOM file nothing reads prev_pos but filemap_read()
itself: readahead is forced and returns before looking at it.  Skipping
the store there takes a small hot table at 64 threads from 10.7M to
14.1M Gets/s, against 12.5M with the series as posted.

I will replace this patch with that.

-- 
  Kiryl Shutsemau / Kirill A. Shutemov
